Up And Down

PermutationsSequencesCounting
Game: Ten numbers stand in a row with some of them hidden. The hidden numbers always go steadily up or steadily down.
How to play: Press a blank card to peek at its number, or choose "Hidden part" to see the whole hidden run. Tick Training for five numbers, and press Reset for a new row.

The colour tells you which way the hidden run goes: red rises, blue falls.

Look for the math

At first you see only part of a permutation of 1 to 10. The missing cards are not chosen at random: they form a run that never turns around. The colour of the cards you can see is a clue to which way that run goes.

A run that never turns

Read left to right, the hidden numbers are either all bigger than the one before (the applet calls them red) or all smaller (blue). Because at least four of the ten are hidden, at most six are shown; with five training numbers, at least three are hidden and at most two are shown. The logic test found that the applet sometimes hides even more than four (even nine!) — so "at most six shown" is always true, but "exactly six" would not be.

Why a run must be there

Write beside each number two counts: the length of the longest rising run ending there, and the longest falling run ending there. Two positions cannot have the same pair of counts: going right, a bigger number raises the first count and a smaller one raises the second. If neither run ever reached 4, both counts would be only 1, 2 or 3, giving just 3 × 3 = 9 different pairs for ten positions. Ten objects in nine boxes force a repeat: that is the pigeonhole principle, called Dirichlet's box principle on the original page.

How far the idea goes

The Erdős–Szekeres theorem says that (r-1)(s-1)+1 distinct numbers force a rising run of r or a falling run of s. For ten numbers take r = s = 4: 3 × 3 + 1 = 10. For five take r = s = 3: 2 × 2 + 1 = 5. Both bounds are sharp: the test checked all 10! = 3,628,800 permutations of ten numbers and all 120 of five, and found a nine-number row (3, 2, 1, 6, 5, 4, 9, 8, 7) with no run of 4, and a four-number row with no run of 3.

Which run gets hidden

The applet tosses a coin to decide whether to look for a rising run or a falling run first. It scans left to right, tries the next bigger (or smaller) number it can find, and keeps the first run that reaches the needed length — then extends that run as far as it can. That is a search for an increasing subsequence (or a falling one), but not always the longest possible one; extending it is why the hidden part can be longer than the minimum. The logic test compares this choice with a second, literal reading of the applet's bytecode for every five-card deal and a large sample of ten-card deals.

Try Training: with only five cards, can you name all three hidden numbers before pressing "Hidden part"? Then look for a ten-card row where only one number is left showing.
